title: Trifferent codes: an exponential improvement over (3/2)^n
credit: Problem posed by Korner and Marton (1988) / Elias; status per Bhandari-Khetan (2024)
premise_risks: Lower-bound side moving in 2026 (unrefereed arXiv:2611.11262), but the upper-bound target is untouched
Problem is sometimes informally called 'the trifference problem' (non-person name) - fine
plain: A set of words of length n over the alphabet {0,1,2} is trifferent if any three distinct words have a position where they show all three letters 0, 1, 2. Let T(n) be the largest size of such a set. A simple counting argument from 1988 gives T(n) ≤ 2(3/2)^n, and every later improvement has been only by a polynomial factor. Show that T(n) ≤ c^n for some constant c < 3/2 and all large n.
math: Call $C\subseteq\{0,1,2\}^n$ trifferent if for all pairwise distinct $x,y,z\in C$ there is $i$ with $\{x_i,y_i,z_i\}=\{0,1,2\}$, and let $T(n)$ be the maximum size of a trifferent code. Prove that $\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log T(n)<\log\frac32$.
